title: Unique Games: is near-satisfiability NP-hard to distinguish from low value?
formal: For every pair of rational constants ε,δ>0 with ε+δ<1, does there exist an integer q≥2 such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon$ from instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta$? Here q is the alphabet size, fixed independently of the input graph, and val(G) is the largest fraction of constraints simultaneously satisfied by any labeling.
definitions: An instance has finitely many vertices and a nonempty explicit list E of directed edges between distinct vertices; repeated edges are allowed and counted separately. Every vertex receives a label in [q]={1,…,q}. An edge e=(u,v) carries an explicitly given permutation π_e:[q]→[q] and is satisfied exactly when π_e(ℓ(u))=ℓ(v). Thus val(G)=max_ℓ |{e satisfied by ℓ}|/|E|. There are no graph expansion or degree promises. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT mapping every satisfiable formula into the ≥1−ε case and every unsatisfiable formula into the ≤δ case. The reduction, its running-time exponent, and q may depend on ε,δ. Inputs with value strictly between the thresholds are outside the promise. The question is the NP-hardness proposition itself; P≠NP is needed when drawing the usual conclusion that no polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm exists.
answer_criterion: Prove the quantified NP-hardness statement, or prove that for some ε,δ every fixed alphabet q fails to give that NP-hardness. A polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm for each q at one fixed pair ε,δ would refute the conjecture assuming P≠NP. Merely improving algorithms on a special graph class, or giving a subexponential algorithm, does not settle it.
context:
Each constraint is locally simple: fixing either endpoint label determines exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. On an instance where every constraint can be satisfied, try each possible label at a component’s root and propagate labels along its edges. Consistency checks then decide perfect satisfiability in polynomial time. Allowing a small fraction of constraints to fail changes the question sharply.

The conjecture says that an instance admitting an almost perfect assignment can nevertheless be hard to distinguish from one where every assignment fails almost everywhere. These are two promised regimes, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum. The alphabet is allowed to grow as the desired gap becomes more demanding. Indeed, a uniformly random labeling satisfies a 1/q fraction in expectation, so a soundness threshold below 1/q is impossible.

This is useful as a starting point for reductions. One replaces a Unique Games constraint by a small optimization gadget, transferring its value gap to a target problem. Raghavendra’s theorem connects such reductions to a general semidefinite-programming framework: under UGC, that framework achieves the approximation thresholds of fixed finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems, to arbitrary constant accuracy.

The strongest relevant hardness milestone must be read with its completeness parameter. The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies hardness for Unique Games with value at least one half versus arbitrarily small value. It does not make the yes instances almost perfectly satisfiable. Raising completeness from one half to arbitrarily close to one is precisely a remaining gap relevant to this card.

Algorithmic progress also matters even when it is slower than polynomial time. Subexponential algorithms exploit spectral decompositions of the constraint graph, limiting what quantitative hardness reductions could establish. Because a polynomial reduction can enlarge the instance by a parameter-dependent power, these algorithms coexist with the NP-hardness conjecture.
why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.

importance.reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.

progress.text: Khot proposes the conjecture. Perfect satisfiability is polynomial-time decidable; the conjectured hard regime has positive completeness error and an alphabet depending on both gap parameters.

Raghavendra gives a general SDP and rounding framework for fixed finite-domain CSPs and transfers SDP integrality gaps to Unique-Games-based hardness. Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless P=NP.

Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute α>0, an exp(q n^(ε^α))-time algorithm finding a (1−ε^α)-satisfying labeling in a (1−ε)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. In the small fixed-ε regime this is subexponential, but not polynomial.

The line of work proving the 2-to-2 Games Theorem yields NP-hardness of Unique Games at completeness 1/2 and arbitrarily small soundness. Khot’s exposition states this explicitly as Theorem 2.20; it leaves the near-one completeness of UGC unresolved.

The journal version of Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, and Safra’s second installment documents its role in the proof sequence, while retaining the full Unique Games statement as Conjecture 1.4. Its publication is not a new proof of full UGC.

status_note: The 2025 journal account distinguishes the proved 2-to-2 theorem from full UGC. No resolution of the quantified near-one-completeness statement was located in the primary-source search through 10 September 2026.
